title: Lacks v. Lacks (1976)
summary: Failure to satisfy New York’s divorce-residence condition did not make the judgment void for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
notes:
Capron illustrates genuine missing federal jurisdiction. Lacks shows why the label must be justified. Later notes concerning Arbaugh and other statutory requirements develop this distinction in federal law.

The husband's divorce judgment (March 1970) was affirmed by the Appellate Division in 1972; two years later the wife moved to vacate it for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction because the husband had not met the residence requirement. The Court of Appeals held the residence requirements go to the substance of the cause of action, not the court's competence.

sections.Parties: The parties were former spouses litigating the validity of a New York divorce judgment. The later challenge asserted that the statutory residence requirements had not been met.
sections.Material Facts: The divorce action proceeded in the New York Supreme Court, a court of general jurisdiction. A party later attempted to undo the decree by describing noncompliance with the residence statute as a defect in the court’s subject-matter power. The challenge arose after the judgment had become final, making the distinction between an erroneous decision and a void judgment decisive.
sections.Procedural History: The New York Court of Appeals rejected the jurisdictional characterization and the corresponding late effort to invalidate the decree. The assigned materials introduce the case as a warning about imprecise uses of “jurisdiction.”
sections.Issue: Did the residence condition define the court’s competence to hear a divorce case, or was it a requirement affecting the entitlement to a divorce within an otherwise competent court?
sections.Holding: It was the latter. Failure to satisfy that condition did not deprive the court of subject-matter jurisdiction over the class of case.
sections.Reasoning: The Supreme Court’s broad competence over civil actions was distinct from the elements or statutory prerequisites needed to obtain a particular judgment. If every mistaken determination of such a condition destroyed jurisdiction, ordinary errors could be relabeled as grounds for unlimited attacks on final judgments. The court instead asked what kind of authority the statute actually limited. This preserved the distinction between a court lacking power to adjudicate and a court making an error while exercising existing power.

learning.why: Failure to satisfy New York’s divorce-residence condition did not make the judgment void for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

topics.cp-subject-matter: The court distinguished competence over divorce actions from failure to satisfy a particular statutory condition.
topics.cp-procedure-merits: Calling a requirement jurisdictional does not settle whether its violation makes a judgment void.
topics.cp-finality: The attempted late attack threatened a judgment already final on the merits.
topics.cp-collateral: The wife's motion to vacate a final divorce judgment years later is a collateral attack, and the case shows why only true subject-matter defects survive finality.
